Learning objectives Understand the core engineering invariant, work through a bounded example, identify what Umicom Framework already implements and distinguish verified facts from proposed improvements. 1. The idea from first principles An attention key is not necessarily a function of the token ID alone. In a first Transformer block, a key may be projected from a fixed token embedding and a fixed position encoding. In a second block, the key is projected from the output of the first block. That output has already incorporated earlier context through causal attention. Imagine a window with tokens A B C D. The first block computes representations for all four positions. When A is removed, the visible window becomes B C D E. A fresh calculation for B may no longer include A. But a cached second-block representation of B originally contained some influence from A. Reusing it and recomputing it from the truncated window are different computations, even when position encodings are rotary. RoPE makes position-dependent query/key comparisons possible without relabelling retained absolute indices; it does not erase earlier information from already-computed upper-layer states. A multi-layer cache needs a precise context policy: preserve historical hidden states, or recompute truncated-window states and compare under the new policy. Neither policy can be mixed silently with old checkpoints. 2. Connect the lesson to Umicom Framework The Framework's UmiAiTrainingStackedDecoderLogits remains the numerical reference for a complete fixed context. Its current streaming service recomputes that context at every step; it does not claim a qualified multi-layer cache. Keep the existing single-block UmiAiTrainingRotaryWindow research separate from a stacked decoder. A credible test records the checkpoint identity, chosen positional semantics, prompt tokens, window length and exact logits at the eviction boundary. Compare every vocabulary logit, not only the most likely token. Use finite tolerances chosen before inspecting results. 3. Practice Question: When the first token disappears from a three-layer model, why might the cached key for a surviving token in layer three disagree with a freshly recomputed key? Reveal the worked answer Its layer-three input depends on earlier layers that may already contain information from the removed token. Fixed rotary angles alone do not make these hidden-state histories equivalent. Learning objectives Understand the core engineering invariant, work through a bounded example, identify what Umicom Framework already implements and distinguish verified facts from proposed improvements. 1. The idea from first principles Inference usually begins with prefill: evaluate the supplied prompt to establish the model state needed for its next prediction. Then decode one token at a time. Both phases use the model, but their shapes and performance characteristics can differ. For a model with four layers, eight prompt tokens and six generated tokens, a straightforward complete-context implementation performs eight token rows through each layer for every generation step. That is 4 × 8 × 6 = 192 token-layer rows. This does not count embeddings, the vocabulary projection, or the varying attention-score work. If a genuinely qualified incremental cache could preserve all eight prompt positions and append only the five sampled tokens needed to produce six outputs, its optimistic token-layer count would be (8 + 5) × 4 = 52. This is hypothetical: the present stacked decoder does not provide that cache, and whether it is equivalent depends on model architecture and context-eviction semantics. Report time to first token, prefill latency, inter-token latency and total elapsed time separately. Reducing a row count is not itself proof of a speed improvement. 2. Connect the lesson to Umicom Framework The Framework's UmiAiTrainingStackedGenerationSessionInspect reports computedFullContextTokenRows and computedTransformerTokenLayerRows for the current full-context implementation. The statistic describes requested work; it does not measure elapsed time or permit the application to claim a speculative cache was used. Use UmiAiTrainingStackedGenerationSessionCreate, Next, Inspect and Destroy according to the existing borrowed-model lifetime contract. Do not train or destroy the model while a session exists. 3. Practice Question: Why are there only five appended output tokens when six tokens are sampled, and why is 52 not an observed Framework benchmark? Reveal the worked answer The final token is sampled from the current state but need not be appended unless another sample is requested. The 52-row result assumes a future qualified cache; the current stacked generator recomputes full contexts. Learning objectives Understand the core engineering invariant, work through a bounded example, identify what Umicom Framework already implements and distinguish verified facts from proposed improvements. 1. The idea from first principles A model checkpoint contains a particular family of weights. The input-construction policy decides where the prompt tokens appear, which special token is used for padding, and when a context rolls. These are separate aspects of reproducibility. Consider a four-position decoder receiving two token IDs, 10 and 11. A left-padded input might be [BOS, BOS, 10, 11], whereas a growing-prefix input begins [10, 11] at position zero. A model with learned absolute positions is allowed to give different predictions in these two cases. Giving both results the same checkpoint hash does not mean they are numerically comparable. Learning objectives Understand the core engineering invariant, work through a bounded example, identify what Umicom Framework already implements and distinguish verified facts from proposed improvements. 1. The idea from first principles A newly implemented multi-layer cache should be measured at the exact transition where the context first becomes full and an old token is evicted. A cache that only passes short-prefix tests may silently return stale hidden states after that point. Design three controlled input families: a prefix shorter than the context, a prefix exactly at capacity, and a sequence which extends at least two tokens beyond capacity. Use fixed, finite parameters and token IDs. Independently run the canonical complete-context decoder on the reference input for each state. For every step compare the full vocabulary logits with a predeclared absolute and, where appropriate, relative tolerance. Also compare predicted token IDs and checkpoint bytes; these are different checks. The test must reject a non-finite logit even if another path produces the same non-finite value. Do not assume that matching only final sampled words proves equal probability distributions. Two vectors can have the same largest index yet materially different other scores. 2. Connect the lesson to Umicom Framework Keep the canonical UmiAiTrainingStackedDecoderLogits implementation unchanged as an independent reference. Only after an opt-in candidate demonstrates parity in the precise model semantics should a performance benchmark compare it with that reference. Learning objectives Understand the core engineering invariant, work through a bounded example, identify what Umicom Framework already implements and distinguish verified facts from proposed improvements. 1. The idea from first principles Memory use can increase when inference avoids recomputing work. A KV cache retains two arrays—keys and values—for each transformer layer and retained token. With a full-width representation, a simple FP32 estimate is 2 × layers × tokens × channels × 4 bytes × concurrent sequences. For three layers, context length 16, width 32 and two simultaneous conversations, the payload estimate is 2 × 3 × 16 × 32 × 4 × 2 = 24,576 bytes. This excludes metadata, fragmentation, attention scores, hidden states, queueing, allocator overhead and any temporary buffers. It is a payload estimate, not a sufficient process-memory budget. Attention computation also depends on context length: each new query compares against all retained keys. A cache can avoid repeating old projections but still performs dot products for new queries. When extending context, always calculate both memory requirements and expected attention work. 2. Connect the lesson to Umicom Framework The Framework already provides UmiAiTrainingModelScalingEstimateBuild for proposed model shapes. Use its kvCacheFp32Bytes as an estimate for the stated full-channel layout; its documentation explicitly excludes many runtime allocations. For live, small-scale measurements, use the existing tape's UmiAiTrainingTapeMemoryInspect and keep its tracked allocations distinct from process RSS. Memory allocation and release remain Framework-owned. An application must not implement its own hidden matrix allocator to compensate for an underestimated budget. 3. Practice Question: Using the same formula, how much FP32 KV payload would four layers, eight tokens, 16 channels and one sequence need? Reveal the worked answer 2 × 4 × 8 × 16 × 4 × 1 = 4,096 bytes. Learning objectives Understand the core engineering invariant, work through a bounded example, identify what Umicom Framework already implements and distinguish verified facts from proposed improvements. 1. The idea from first principles Umicom's original educational tokeniser maps every raw byte to one token ID by adding four to the byte value. Four other IDs are reserved. It is fully reversible and simple to inspect, but many words require several byte tokens. A multi-byte UTF-8 character occupies several bytes, so one printable character may also occupy several tokens. The tokenisation choice changes sequence lengths, context usage and dataset handling. If a hypothetical subword tokeniser converts a sentence into 18 tokens while the byte tokeniser requires 44 bytes, the same 32-token context can hold the first representation but not the second. That does not prove the subword model is better: it changes the trained vocabulary and the embedding/output matrix dimensions. Vocabulary changes also affect checkpoint identity. A decoder trained with byte IDs cannot be loaded as though its embeddings represented a newly trained subword vocabulary. A larger tokeniser requires an explicit, versioned token-to-ID contract and separately trained weights. 2. Connect the lesson to Umicom Framework The existing UmiAiByteEncode and UmiAiByteDecode are the canonical reversible byte operations. Do not reimplement byte-to-token arithmetic in Studio or Bits2Banking application logic. Any future tokenizer belongs in Framework and needs special-token tests, Unicode/input-format policy, deterministic merges, vocabulary hashing and memory bounds. A training dataset must preserve reviewed source rights regardless of how tokens are represented. 3. Practice Question: If the raw UTF-8 text occupies 45 bytes, how many ordinary byte tokens does the existing reversible tokenizer emit? Reveal the worked answer Exactly 45 ordinary token IDs. The caller may choose to add separate BOS/EOS IDs, but they are not inserted implicitly by the byte encoding call. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation Author: Sammy Hegab · Implementation language: C23 Learning objectives Understand the encoding and ownership invariant, follow a concrete example, identify the reusable Framework service and explain a safe failure outcome. 1. The engineering problem A byte-token language model emits one raw byte at a time. One printed character, however, may need two, three or four UTF-8 bytes. If an application displays each byte immediately as a character, it can show corrupted text or introduce replacement symbols that were not in the model output. The native Framework therefore provides UmiUtf8StreamAppend. It owns no model: it accepts one byte and emits a complete UTF-8 scalar sequence only when enough valid bytes have arrived. The generated bytes themselves remain under the existing Framework tokenizer and stacked inference interfaces. Consider the euro symbol €, encoded in UTF-8 as hexadecimal bytes E2 82 AC. The first call accepts E2 and reports zero completed output bytes. The second accepts 82 and also reports zero. The third accepts AC and publishes all three bytes in order. The caller must use the reported length rather than strlen because streaming data is not a NUL-terminated C string. 2. Use the existing Framework boundaries #include "umicom/base/utf8_stream.h" UmiUtf8Stream utf8 = {0}; uint8_t completed[4] = {0}; size_t completedBytes = 0U; UmiUtf8StreamReset(&utf8); /* A real caller obtains one byte from the Framework inference session. */ UmiStatus status = UmiUtf8StreamAppend( &utf8, (uint8_t)0xe2U, completed, sizeof(completed), &completedBytes); /* status == UMI_STATUS_OK; completedBytes == 0. */ The application does not reinterpret partial UTF-8 as text. The Framework rejects overlong byte sequences, UTF-16 surrogate encodings and code points above U+10FFFF. Invalid input leaves the stream and output unchanged. It does not invent replacement characters. Practice Question: Why is it incorrect to display E2 as an independent UTF-8 character? Reveal the worked answer It is only the start byte of a three-byte code-point encoding; valid display requires the continuation bytes 82 AC too. The engineering problem A generative model can stop after any byte. It may end with a complete character, or it may stop while the first or second byte of a multi-byte character is still pending. A well-behaved UI must not silently claim the pending prefix is a complete UTF-8 string. UmiUtf8StreamFinish checks that no incomplete scalar remains. If the stream contains only the initial F0 byte of a four-byte emoji sequence, the call reports UMI_STATUS_INVALID_STATE. That is a validation result, not an instruction to emit fake text. The caller can preserve the original bytes for audit, report the truncated text to the user or apply a separately approved display policy. Model generation cancellation and Unicode validation are also different actions. Destroying a stacked-generation session stops sampling; it does not automatically make the last partial UTF-8 prefix valid. 2. Use the existing Framework boundaries The Framework-owned UmiAiTrainingStackedGenerationSessionDestroy cancels token generation. UmiUtf8StreamReset starts a fresh text-validation stream for another answer. The caller should keep those lifetimes distinct, because resetting one component must not alter the borrowed model, its checkpoint or an unrelated output. Never treat U+0000 as a C terminator just because it is valid UTF-8. Buffer capacity and reported byte count remain mandatory when handing the generated bytes to a GTK widget or to another Framework text service. Learning objective: Specify the boundary of an attention operator that computes the newest query only, without changing the established Transformer model. 1. Understand the problem The last inference batch introduced a true incremental projection path, but its attention composition still handles unnecessary earlier query rows. The next optimisation is narrower: given one newly calculated query for each head, attend to keys and values representing only the permitted causal prefix. The output is one vector per head, not an entire sequence of attention rows. This is an execution optimisation, not a change to the learned weights or the model’s probability distribution. A proposed C23 Framework interface must make input shapes, ownership, validity lengths, model identity and status explicit. It must not own token sampling, mutate K/V storage, advance a session cursor, or choose new positional embeddings. Those actions belong to the established Framework execution and session services. The output must be fully defined on success and not exposed as valid on failure. 2. Fully worked example Assume 4 heads, head width 8 and a valid prefix of 6 tokens. A candidate reads one Q[4,8], one K[4,6,8] and one V[4,6,8], and proposes A[4,8]. That is 32 query elements, 192 key elements, 192 value elements and 32 output elements. At FP32, the three inputs alone occupy (32 + 192 + 192) × 4 = 1,664 bytes; this number excludes scratch buffers, model weights and allocator overhead. The candidate must not silently use a seventh padded row: a physical capacity of 8 does not mean eight valid keys. 3. Engineering verification and connection to Umicom Framework A design review must reject a zero valid length, mismatched head count, invalid stride, arithmetic overflow, nonfinite unmasked inputs and overlapping buffers when aliasing is unsupported. On success, check output shape = [heads, head_width]; on failure, check the cache version, sampling state and token history remain unchanged. These are proposed acceptance requirements, not claims that a new public ABI exists. The existing Umicom Framework decoder, training tape and K/V ownership services remain the authority for implementation. This educational lesson specifies behaviour; it does not introduce a competing application-local inference engine or claim that the proposed single-query kernel is already merged or performance-qualified. 4. Mathematics connection Review Mathematics for AI — Unit 125. The mathematics companion includes a calculation that can be verified independently of a compiled model. 5. Exercise Question: Why must validPrefixLength be separate from the storage capacity? Reveal the worked answer Capacity describes how many rows fit in memory; the valid length says how many causal keys may contribute to the current query. Learning objective: Compute scaled dot products, softmax probabilities and the weighted value vector by hand. 1. Understand the problem For one head, take a query vector q of width d, keys k_0 … k_t, and value vectors v_0 … v_t. Score key i with s_i = dot(q, k_i) / sqrt(d). Apply softmax across only the valid, unmasked keys and return sum_i probability_i × v_i. A causal decoder’s newest query normally sees every retained key and itself; there are no future keys in the accepted prefix. Learning objective: Track the shape and ordering of the attention result before the residual connection. 1. Understand the problem Multi-head attention is not a simple average of heads. Each head produces a vector of width d_h; these vectors are concatenated in model-defined head order to form a width-d_model vector when d_model = heads × d_h. The established output-projection matrix then transforms that concatenated vector, after which the correct residual, normalisation and feed-forward sequence continues. An optimiser that computes each head correctly but changes concatenation order can alter the whole model. The candidate may optimise the way data moves, but it must not change learned matrices, transposes, activation functions or arithmetic operation ordering without an explicitly qualified equivalence. 2. Fully worked example For two heads of width two, outputs h0=(0.8,0.4) and h1=(0.1,-0.2) concatenate to (0.8,0.4,0.1,-0.2). Swapping the heads gives (0.1,-0.2,0.8,0.4). Learning objective: Separate cache correctness from memory safety and checkpoint trust. 1. Understand the problem A K/V cache holds derived representations of one particular frozen model state. Matching tensor dimensions does not authorise reuse after a weight update. Learning objective First-token latency and subsequent-token latency measure different phases; neither is captured by an undifferentiated token-layer counter. Understand the mechanism A decoder receives a prompt before it can emit a token. During prefill, it evaluates the incoming prompt and prepares any reusable key/value projections. The first token can be sampled from the last prompt-position logit row. During decode, the model accepts each newly sampled token and produces the next distribution. A KV cache changes the work of later steps, not the need to process a previously unseen prompt. In a streamed application the time to the first emitted token includes more than prefill: admission, queueing, transfers, sampler work and any retrieval may contribute. In a local synchronous test, those services are absent, so report exactly what the timer covers. The existing Umicom prefix generator runs full-context calculations. The cached generator can reuse K/V while a prefix grows, but learned-absolute-position rollover forces a canonical rebuild. Measure each regime separately instead of reporting one average as the universal property of the model. This distinction is especially important when a four-token educational context rolls over far more often than a realistic model with a long context. Fully worked example Assume 3 ms to create the session and evaluate the prompt, then 2 ms for each of four subsequent decode transitions. A five-token stream occupies about 11 ms of compute and orchestration: 3 + (4 × 2). The first-token wait is 3 ms in this simplified laboratory. Average end-to-end latency per token is 11 / 5 = 2.2 ms; it is neither the first-token delay nor the 2 ms transition time. Native C23 laboratory Make a timeline that separates session creation, the first generated token, pending-token processing and every later sample. Annotate any position-rollover event. Do not label the total native benchmark runtime as TTFT when it measures an entire generation call. The numerical and inference services are owned by Umicom Framework. Existing samplers, stacked decoder, K/V store and training tape remain authoritative. Where this lesson discusses a proposed capability, it is labelled as a design rather than a verified implementation. No numerical equivalence or runtime acceleration is inferred merely from an operation count. Connect the mathematics See Mathematics Unit 161 for the corresponding numerical reasoning and a worked exercise. Learning objective An elapsed wall-clock timer is not the same as process CPU time or a theoretical operation counter. Understand the mechanism A defensible local measurement records a start instant immediately before the operation being compared and an end instant immediately after it. Operating systems may interrupt a process while the timer runs. That is not an error: the interruption forms part of observed wall-clock latency. The timing source should be monotonic so that wall-clock corrections do not create negative durations. On Windows a native program can use QueryPerformanceCounter; on POSIX systems it can use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC). Elapsed calls include allocation, checkpoint identity verification, prefill, token generation, cache rollover and destruction when all of those operations lie inside the timed boundary. Recording only the inner matrix multiplication cannot justify claims about complete prompt responses. Always state the boundary and whether model construction and weight loading are excluded. Native code can collect these timestamps without a PowerShell or Python runtime. Fully worked example A timer produces start = 7,000,000,000 ns and end = 7,018,000,000 ns. Subtraction gives 18,000,000 ns, equal to 18 ms. A second trial returns 15 ms. Reporting only the 15 ms fastest run hides scheduling variation; preserve the full sample set and calculate a robust summary. Learning objective Running every canonical trial first may bias timings through cache warming, CPU frequency and memory pressure. Understand the mechanism Run an untimed warmup for each path. Then alternate execution order across measured pairs: reference → cached, followed by cached → reference. This is counterbalancing. It reduces one systematic source of bias, although it cannot control operating-system scheduling, temperature or other processes. Record compilation mode and device information alongside results. The educational Framework service uses bounded warmups and measured pairs, deliberately alternating order. A short laboratory with five pairs illustrates the procedure but does not support an inference about every computer or prompt. Longer studies should use multiple independent processes, workload order randomisation where appropriate and variation measurements. Keep reproducibility (fixed model and seed) separate from temporal determinism: a repeatable output sequence can still have variable elapsed time. Learning objective A median is useful, but not a confidence interval, and a single benchmark run cannot justify a broad speedup claim. Understand the mechanism Sort measurements before selecting their median. For an odd number of readings the median is the middle number; for an even number it is the average of the two central numbers. Learning objective Correctness comparisons should distinguish exact token parity, bounded numerical logit parity and model-identity integrity. Understand the mechanism A cache can preserve the same sampled token while subtly changing the model's predicted probabilities. Learning objective The cache owner accounts for some allocations, not the entire memory consumed by training or inference. Understand the mechanism The K/V cache stores projections across layers and token positions. Its theoretical byte count follows 2 × layers × tokens × KV-heads × head-dimension × bytes-per-element. A concrete cache owner may reserve a full context upfront, so retained-token count and allocated capacity are different quantities. Other memory consumers include model parameters, temporary attention scores, tensor tape nodes, allocator overhead, stacks, loaded libraries and operating-system page mappings. Never call the sum of K/V floats "peak RAM". The Framework's reserved K/V byte counter is a bounded component accounting measurement. Peak resident set size (RSS) requires an operating-system observation of the whole process. A rigorous report presents both rather than mixing them. For more advanced models, sliding windows, grouped-query attention and quantisation change the cache shape; measure the exact representation, not an assumed FP32 dense MHA layout. Fully worked example Two layers, eight KV channels, six context positions and FP32 values require 2 × 2 × 8 × 6 × 4 = 768 bytes of K/V payload. The process may occupy many megabytes even though this particular cache reports 768 bytes. Learning objective The learned absolute position policy forces full recomputation after eviction, so cache benefits depend on prompt and generation lengths. Understand the mechanism Incremental reuse is valid while earlier tokens keep their absolute position indices. A prompt of length two in a six-token context can append four new positions without changing previous indices. Once the window is full, evicting the oldest token shifts every remaining token to a new learned position. This changes its embedding and propagates through all Transformer layers. Reusing old K/V rows after that shift would be mathematically unsound. Measure growth-phase steps and rollover-phase steps independently. A short-context educational benchmark may spend most of its generation in full rebuilds, making cached inference slower overall despite one-query attention being cheaper during growth. Report the first rollover and at least one repeated rollover; otherwise the test does not cover its dominant correctness boundary. Fully worked example Context = 6, initial prompt = 2, generated outputs = 8. The first generated ID comes from prefill, so there are seven pending-token transitions. Four transitions extend the prefix from 2 → 6. The remaining three transitions rebuild a rolled six-token window. In a model with two layers, each rebuild evaluates 6 × 2 token-layer rows. Learning objective Throughput for many requests is not the same performance metric as latency for one request. Understand the mechanism A batched inference engine may share a model's weight buffers across sessions but each request has its own token history, sampler state and K/V ownership. Continuous batching admits and completes requests at different times; this can improve aggregate device utilisation, especially on accelerators. It can also increase queueing or time-to-first-token for a short request behind long work. The present Umicom educational stacked session is synchronous, bounded and caller-serialised. It is not a continuous-batching scheduler. Before adding one, define per-request ownership, fairness, bounded queues, cancellation and model identity. Request isolation is a correctness property, not only a performance feature: mixing K/V rows from different prompts creates cross-session information leakage. A scheduler must never treat one request's position count as another's. Fully worked example A device serves four requests in 200 ms and emits 80 tokens across them. Aggregate throughput is 80 / 0.2 = 400 tokens/s. A single user could still wait 150 ms for their first token; aggregate throughput does not describe that experience. Learning objective Prefix reuse requires identical tokens, model weights, positional policy and cache shape, plus explicit lifetime management. Learning objective Grouped-query attention reduces the number of K/V heads without removing query heads. Understand the mechanism In ordinary multi-head attention the model commonly has one independent K and V projection per query head. Grouped-query attention (GQA) allows several query heads to share one K/V head, reducing retained projections and memory bandwidth. It changes the model's parameter shapes and attention mapping. It is not an optimisation that can be enabled by simply dropping rows from a checkpoint trained for standard MHA. The native educational stacked decoder uses its original attention-head and projection layout. That checkpoint family remains unchanged. Future GQA support needs a separate architecture identifier, explicit head-to-KV mapping, shape-aware persistence and independent numerical qualification. This lesson treats the memory equations as a planning tool rather than claiming current production support. Fully worked example With 16 query heads, 4 KV heads, head width 64, 24 layers, 4,096 tokens and two FP16 bytes per value, GQA K/V payload is 2 × 24 × 4,096 × 4 × 64 × 2 = 100,663,296 bytes ≈ 96 MiB per sequence. Standard MHA with 16 KV heads would be about 384 MiB, four times larger. Native C23 laboratory Calculate the payload for 8,192 tokens and 8 KV heads under the same layer count and precision. Learning objective Reducing stored precision saves bytes, but requires explicit rounding rules and end-to-end quality checks. Understand the mechanism A compact K/V representation uses fewer bits per stored scalar. A simple symmetric int8 scheme computes a positive scale from the block's maximum absolute value and rounds each value to a signed integer. Dequantisation reconstructs only an approximation, so attention scores and final logits can change. Real methods differ by scale granularity, treatment of outliers, signed ranges and calibration. Do not mix a quantised cache with the existing FP32 session and silently claim it is numerically identical. Choose a separate cache representation and identify its precision in the checkpoint/runtime contract. Measure memory and actual decode latency; smaller allocations can be offset by dequantisation overhead. For accuracy, use held-out loss/perplexity, full logits and task outcomes. Published KVQuant work illustrates why key/value distributions and outliers matter, but its GPU results are not transferable to the bounded native educational model. Fully worked example For a scalar x = 0.4 and scale s = 0.01, the stored integer round(0.4/0.01) = 40; dequantisation gives 0.4. For x = 0.403, the same scale stores round(40.3) = 40 and reconstructs 0.4, with error −0.003. Some values incur larger errors near saturation. LLM study routeCanonical MarkdownPrevious HTML lessonNext HTML lessonBits to Banking · Umicom Foundation Author: Sammy Hegab Implementation approach: native C23, with Assembly only after justified profiling. Prerequisites: Lessons 377–392, Mathematics Unit 245. Learning outcomes Explain design round-scoped native learning jobs, identify the exact boundary between evidence, model arithmetic and coordination, and design at least one test that can fail. Distinguish implemented Umicom source from suggested research. Concept and mechanism A federated training job is not merely a queue entry. It pins an initial model checkpoint, data-use policy, worker identity, dataset shard and numerical aggregation rule to one synchronisation round. All workers in an ordinary FedAvg round must begin from the same tensor layout and base state. The coordinator allocates a finite step and sample budget before any update is considered for aggregation. Different initial checkpoints produce deltas that cannot safely be combined as if they share a common origin. A correct research system starts with the immutable experiment contract: a common base checkpoint, authorised dataset partitions, an explicit sample-count rule, a deterministic round identifier and a preregistered evaluation metric. Distributed operation also requires stated concurrency, failure and network assumptions. The mathematical candidate resulting from averaging does not become an approved model checkpoint without an independent quality gate. Worked scenario Consider three workers, each given checkpoint hash A, 12 local steps and one authorised shard. Worker B returns a delta labelled hash B instead. Comparing 32 digest bytes can reject a mismatched label before the numerical stage, but cannot prove that A was honestly used. A genuine training/replay check is needed for the stronger claim. What can go wrong? Treating a well-formed digest as proof of training leads to false trust. Likewise, reporting a worker count without a round identifier makes stale work indistinguishable from fresh contributions. Native Umicom engineering connection The Framework's established UmiAiTrainingFederatedRound is the sole numeric FedAvg-delta owner. The additive UmiAiTrainingFederatedJob admission component tracks one round of assignments and routes accepted full FP32 deltas through that existing numeric API. It does not train remote workers, sign contributions, verify dataset rights, provide Byzantine resilience, implement secure aggregation or run blockchain consensus. The remaining training, checkpoint, messaging and governance functions must be composed from reviewed Framework capabilities rather than duplicated in application code. Umicom Framework owns the job state; Studio and LLM workbenches only display its inspected state. Verification exercise Reproduce the worked case using synthetic inputs. Then reject an invalid, stale, mismatched or adversarial input without changing the accepted aggregate. Report the exact result and a separate list of work not measured: real network RTT, GPU hours, held-out model improvement and privacy guarantee. Question: What must be pinned before a round can combine three workers? Reveal the worked answer The shared base checkpoint and tensor schema, training configuration, permitted dataset shards and a defined round identity. Authorisation and real worker computation are separately checked. Mathematics connection Mathematics for AI — Unit 245 provides a quantitative counterpart. ← Lesson 92 · Lesson 94 → · LLM course 1. What does “passed” mean?An application may compile successfully without calculating the right answer. A test may be not run, may fail, or may pass. We must not turn the first two outcomes into a passing result. This lesson introduces a bounded Framework acceptance contract, not a second testing engine. 2. Three real tests that must runTestBusiness analogyEngineering questionGradientsRecalculate the totals on a financial report independentlyDo the derivatives agree with finite differences?Memory budgetA payment must not partially post if funds are unavailableDoes failure preserve the previous tape state?RewindRepeatedly opening a saved document must not duplicate its contentsDoes each cycle restore retained allocations? 3. Formula explainederror = |analytical gradient − numerical gradient|A gradient is a number describing how changing a model weight changes the loss. The vertical bars mean absolute value—ignore whether the difference is positive or negative. If the analytical gradient is 0.0234 and the numerical gradient is 0.0231, error = 0.0003. If the approved threshold is 0.0008, then 0.0003 is within the permitted difference.Need a slower explanation? Open Maths Unit 14 or Maths Unit 19. 4. Native C23 contract#include "umicom/ai/training/rotary_acceptance.h" /* The three observations below are ILLUSTRATIVE. They are not actual CTest results. */ UmiAiTrainingRotaryAcceptanceObservation example[3] = { {0U, 1, 1, 72U, 0.0003}, {1U, 1, 1, 6U, 0.0}, {2U, 1, 1, 48U, 0.0} }; UmiAiTrainingRotaryAcceptanceReport report; UmiStatus status = UmiAiTrainingRotaryAcceptanceEvaluate( example, 3U, 0.0008, &report); /* report.accepted describes ONLY the supplied example evidence. */The function never executes the real tests. They must already have run through CTest or the Framework's test service. Passing its fixture regression proves only that the interpreter accepts valid records and rejects bad ones. 5. PracticeWhich outcome should be recorded if the gradients test never executed but the memory and rewind tests passed? Why is “two out of three passed” not sufficient to approve an optimisation?Show answerThe evidence is incomplete; the acceptance gate must not approve the release. A missing gradient test leaves numerical correctness unverified.

← Lesson 93 · LLM course1. Why not optimise immediately?In banking software, a faster ledger posting routine is not an improvement if it posts incorrect balances. In an LLM, a faster attention operator is not useful if it produces wrong gradients. First prove correctness using the full Framework training tape. Then measure allocations and speed honestly. 2. What does fusion mean?Imagine a manufacturing line that passes an object through three separate machines, storing an intermediate result between each. Fusion attempts to combine stages and reduce temporary storage. For RoPE attention, a future Framework-owned tape node might combine Q/K rotation and masked attention. This batch does NOT implement or benchmark that fused node. 3. Which gradients must still work?input gradient = R(position)ᵀ × output gradientR(position) is a rotation of two coordinates determined by a token's position. The superscript ᵀ means transpose; for a rotation it reverses the rotation. The multiplication sign means to apply that transformation to the gradient arriving from later layers. If a forward rotation changes [1,0] to [0,1] at a 90° angle, its backward counterpart converts [0,1] to [1,0].For first-principles explanation, study Maths Unit 7 and Unit 20. 4. Safety rulesThe future node must respect two properties: (a) fail without publishing partial tensors and (b) restore the exact live-node count and current tracked bytes after rollback. Historic peak allocation is not expected to decrease. Once the new node is compared numerically against the existing implementation, benchmark under identical model, prompt, hardware and build modes. 5. Practical exampleSuppose old attention uses a temporary 600-byte allocation and a proposed operator uses only 400 bytes for the same work. The absolute saving is 600 − 400 = 200 bytes; the percentage reduction is 200 ÷ 600 × 100 ≈ 33.3%. This is only a worked mathematical example—not a measurement from Umicom.Exercise answerA saving in allocated bytes alone does not prove the program is faster. Measure CPU time, wall time, accuracy, and correctness separately.

← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Distinguish a base-model checkpoint from adapter weights, understand which optimiser data must survive a restart, and identify why a report is not an executable model. By the end, you should be able to draw a safe recovery boundary without relying on a scripting runtime. 1. Start with the three different kinds of state A native language-model application can contain several related but different records. The frozen decoder contains the original token embeddings, position embeddings, Transformer weights and output projection. An adapter contains only smaller trainable matrices inserted into selected attention and feed-forward projections. A training cursor records where to continue in an approved, ordered dataset. If the original model is unchanged, it is wasteful to duplicate it inside every adapter snapshot. More importantly, it is dangerous to load an adapter against a different original model merely because the tensor dimensions happen to fit. The Umicom adapter snapshot therefore binds the adapter to the SHA-256 of the canonical, complete frozen decoder checkpoint. Record What it can restore What it cannot establish Frozen decoder checkpoint Original model weights and training-step identity Permission to use the model Projection-adapter snapshot Selected adapter weights and adapter SGD step count AdamW moments or approved dataset identity Continuation snapshot Adapter snapshot plus dataset digest, training plan and next-example cursor Trusted publisher identity or storage durability Experiment receipt Aggregate measurements and source/model references The trainable weights themselves The existing Framework UmiAiTrainingDecoderProjectionAdapter owns an independent tape, so the original decoder's graph-rewind policy cannot discard the adapter leaves. 2. Why checkpointing is more than saving an array Suppose the model has an eight-token context, channels equal to eight and a rank-two adapter. The adapter consists of two matrices per selected projection. Their dimensions are [inputChannels, rank] and [rank, outputChannels]. If the query weight is 8×8, its rank-two adapter has 8×2 + 2×8 = 32 trainable elements, rather than 64 elements in the full projection. Saving just those 32 numbers is insufficient. The restore operation also needs the projection role, exact rank, original base identity, element representation and order. The portable Framework checkpoint preserves these contracts without serialising a compiler-dependent C structure. 3. The real Framework boundaries Use UmiAiTrainingDecoderProjectionSnapshotSize to calculate required storage, ...Encode to publish the complete encoded snapshot and ...Restore to create a new owned adapter bound to the active frozen decoder. A successful restore must not mutate an existing adapter. Only an in-memory buffer is exported by this API. A caller that saves it to disk must use approved Framework file-publication services, preserve a last-known-good copy and protect access permissions. A single successful memory encoding does not mean a durable disk write succeeded. 4. What a training restart still needs The existing optimiser in this learning path is stateless SGD. Given identical adapter weights, learning rate and next examples, the next updates can be reproduced. AdamW additionally retains moment estimates for each parameter; restarting those estimates at zero changes the optimisation algorithm. The snapshot must therefore not be called an AdamW resume checkpoint. Practice and worked answer Question: If a selected projection is 8×16 and adapter rank is 2, how many adapter elements must be saved? Solution: 8×2 + 2×16 = 16 + 32 = 48 trainable elements. The 8×16 base weights remain frozen and are identified separately. A complete restart must also know where the data cursor stopped. Next: Portable model records and restoring SGD state. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Read an explicit binary format, explain fixed-width integers and checksums, and distinguish accidental corruption detection from publisher authentication. We use a portable native C23 snapshot, not direct memory dumping or an executable script. 1. Why writing a C structure to disk can fail A compiler may insert padding between members of a C struct. An integer can occupy different byte orders on different processor families. A pointer refers to a location in the current process and has no meaning after restart. Consequently, taking sizeof(struct) bytes from memory and treating them as a permanent model file is not an interoperable storage contract. The Framework's adapter snapshot writes a header with explicit offsets, version, projection-selection mask, rank, completed steps and the exact frozen-decoder SHA-256. Its payload contains separate per-projection checkpoints encoded through the existing Framework adapter checkpoint service. A final SHA-256 covers the full preceding record. 2. Read a little-endian integer Suppose a four-byte unsigned integer contains the decimal value 258. Its hexadecimal value is 0x00000102. In little-endian order the bytes are 02 01 00 00. To decode it, multiply the four byte values by powers of 256 and add: 2 + 1×256 + 0 + 0 = 258. A reader should not cast a raw byte pointer to uint32_t * and assume alignment or machine endianness. It must validate the length before accessing the bytes and assemble the value using bounded unsigned arithmetic. 3. A layered integrity check A restored projection passes three distinct questions. First, is the outer record structurally valid with the declared length and digest? Second, does each inner adapter checkpoint have a valid format, finite FP32 weights and matching frozen projection? Third, does the live decoder match the exact checkpoint SHA-256 declared by the snapshot? Only then may a fully constructed adapter become visible to the caller. The whole-record SHA-256 can detect corrupted bytes, but an attacker who can replace both record and digest can calculate a new digest. The Framework must independently authenticate and approve an external file; no unsigned hash can prove who authorised it. 4. Failure atomicity Imagine a valid destination buffer containing the previous snapshot. The new encoded result requires 900 bytes, but its capacity is 850. The service must return UMI_STATUS_CAPACITY_EXCEEDED while leaving all 850 existing bytes and the caller's written-count variable unchanged. A failed restore likewise leaves its output adapter pointer untouched. The implementation stages all bytes privately before the final copy. Partial records must not be presented as successful new snapshots. Practice Question: Why is a SHA-256 value insufficient to trust an arbitrary downloaded model? Answer: It proves only a relationship between the bytes and the digest supplied. It does not establish that a trusted publisher signed or approved those bytes. Question: What should a parser do with an unknown binary-format revision? Answer: Reject it. Guessing a layout could misinterpret roles, step counts or weights. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Understand seeded permutations, global example indices, a committed training step and the difference between a cursor value and updated model weights. Learn why both must be checkpointed as one logical unit. 1. Work through a small training schedule Imagine four approved training examples with global indices [0,2,4,6]. Our deterministic dataset service chooses one permutation for each epoch. The first epoch might visit [4,0,6,2]; the next may be different because the epoch number is part of the seed. The exact order belongs to the Framework dataset service, not to a home-grown shuffle in Umicom Studio. Suppose a run finishes the first two examples in epoch zero. Its cursor is (completedEpochs=0, nextExampleOffset=2). The next training call must retrieve the third entry from the same epoch's deterministic permutation. Starting a new shuffle or skipping to another epoch would be a different training run. 2. Confirm the step-count equation Let T be the number of training examples in each epoch, E the completed whole epochs, O the next-example offset and S0 the adapter's step count when this run started. Then: expectedCurrentAdapterSteps = S0 + E×T + O For S0=5, T=4, E=2, O=3, we expect 5 + 2×4 + 3 = 16 completed adapter steps. This equation is a simple but valuable corruption check. It catches impossible combinations of counter and cursor before another weight update. 3. One update is a precise commit boundary UmiAiTrainingSupervisedContinuationTrainNext uses the existing Framework dataset order, fetches one owned supervised window and delegates the numerical update to UmiAiTrainingDecoderProjectionAdapterTrainStep. Only when this succeeds does it advance the cursor. Previous successful SGD steps are not rolled back if a later call fails. Once all examples in an epoch are consumed, TrainNext refuses another step until ...FinishEpoch performs scheduled held-out evaluation and begins the next epoch. This separate transition prevents accidentally double-training the last example when an evaluation fails. 4. Why the model and cursor must travel together Suppose an old adapter snapshot contains the weights after 10 updates but its cursor says 11. If restored together without validation, the next step will skip one example. Reversing that mismatch repeats an example. The Framework continuation snapshot combines the current adapter weights and cursor into one bounded, integrity-checked record, and restore checks their step counts agree. This is exact continuation only for this stateless SGD policy, using the same approved frozen decoder, same reviewed dataset and same compiler/numerical behaviour expectations. It is not a guarantee of bit-identical results on every CPU implementation. Practice A run begins at step 20, has 3 training examples per epoch and has completed 2 full epochs plus 1 example. Its expected step count is 20 + 2×3 + 1 = 27. If the checkpoint says 28, stop and investigate rather than silently adjusting the cursor. Continue to failure handling. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Separate three states: an attempted update, a committed adapter update and a durably saved checkpoint. Learn what to do when disk I/O, evaluation or a training step fails. 1. A training attempt is not automatically a commit Assume a native training call receives approved next-token targets. It validates the model, source identity, mask and learning rate; constructs its temporary tape graph; computes selected cross-entropy; differentiates it; then asks the established SGD writer to update the adapter parameters. If any calculation fails before the SGD transaction completes, no new training step should be counted. Once the SGD writer returns success, the update is committed in the active in-memory adapter. An error in a later measurement cannot safely pretend that update never happened. The next valid cursor must reflect the weights that actually exist. 2. Evaluate at a clear boundary In the new continuation API, the run deliberately separates TrainNext and FinishEpoch. Training the final example advances the offset to the known training-example count. FinishEpoch carries out the held-out evaluation and transitions to the next epoch. If held-out assessment is unavailable, the training state stays at the end-of-epoch boundary; it does not train that example again. 3. Memory snapshots and durable files are different SnapshotEncode returns one complete native byte array. Successful encoding does not imply that bytes have reached a storage device. A production Umicom application should apply the existing Framework approved-file policy to write a new staging file, flush and publish it safely, keep the earlier known-good snapshot until the new one is verified, and restrict filesystem permissions. Do not teach an application to overwrite its only recovery copy directly. Reopening a file and comparing its digest and complete length can detect accidental damage but cannot prove the source was trusted. An appropriately signed approval is a separate security decision. 4. Predict recovery behaviour Failure point In-memory weights Next safe action Invalid source approval Unchanged Correct review evidence; do not train Insufficient snapshot buffer Unchanged Allocate exact capacity and encode again Invalid loss mask Unchanged Correct window preparation Completed SGD, later evaluation fails Updated Keep committed cursor and retry evaluation Crash after update but before durable snapshot Possibly lost from disk Resume only from the last complete approved snapshot Tampered snapshot Never admitted Recover from independently approved good copy Practice A trainer saved a complete snapshot after 12 updates and then performed 3 more updates before a power failure. The only intact on-disk checkpoint has 12 updates. Can it resume as though 15 updates survived? No. It must restore 12 updates and repeat the subsequent deterministic sequence, or adopt a separately designed durable per-step transaction mechanism. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Build a meaningful regression plan, compare immutable frozen-model bytes, and inspect both exact training replay and held-out quality. Learn what equality does and does not prove. 1. Arrange two fair experiments Create one approved dataset and one frozen native decoder. Make two initial adapters with exactly the same rank, projection-selection flags and initialization seed, or create one adapter snapshot and restore an exact twin. Both paths must start at the same adapter step, dataset SHA-256 and training plan. Path A: train all approved examples and complete all epochs without restarting. Path B: train only one example, export one continuation snapshot, destroy that adapter, restore into a newly owned adapter, and train the remaining examples. Neither path is permitted to change the frozen decoder or reorder the source dataset. 2. Compare the correct objects A high-confidence local restart regression compares the final portable adapter snapshots byte-for-byte. This includes every selected projection's trainable weight values, all role IDs, the exact frozen decoder identity and the committed adapter step. It also compares the final cursor and held-out aggregate metrics under the same build. The test should separately encode the frozen decoder checkpoint before and after training; these bytes must remain unchanged. Since adapter training is meant to leave the original model untouched, a changed decoder checkpoint is a defect, not evidence that the adapter learned more. 3. Check one example of a held-out quality gate Suppose the baseline held-out cross-entropy is 2.30 and the adapted model has 2.05, using the same 100 selected target tokens. The loss difference is 2.05−2.30 = −0.25. If we require an improvement of at least 0.20, that criterion passes. But if baseline top-one accuracy was 0.52 and adapted accuracy is 0.49, a separately required minimum accuracy of 0.50 fails. A responsible quality gate reports the complete decision rather than publishing the favourable loss figure alone. The Framework's UmiAiTrainingSupervisedQualityEvaluate reports observed deltas and policy decisions. A quality acceptance is not a model release authorisation or a test of real-world language understanding. 4. Think about numerical comparisons Two runs on one CPU with the same compiler and deterministic policy should reproduce precisely the same selected order and, subject to the established FP32 implementation, may produce byte-identical checkpoint outputs. That is the acceptance target of this local exercise. Comparisons across different compilers or accelerators may need predeclared numerical tolerances. Never change the tolerance after seeing a failure simply to make the test pass. Record the machine, toolchain and model identity for any performance claim separately. Practice Question: Why isn't a lower training loss enough? Answer: The model might memorise the training examples. The independent held-out evaluation measures different, source-isolated examples; both split integrity and the metric definition must be verified. Next: Run a real native demonstration. A sequence is represented by a table with one row per token and one column per feature. Each Transformer layer stores independent key and value tables. Denote layers by L, retained tokens by T and channels by C. A fully worked example Set L=3, T=4, C=8. One K tensor uses L×T×C = 3×4×8 = 96 float values. V uses another 96, so K+V contains 192 values. At four bytes per FP32 value the raw total is 768 bytes. This excludes model weights and allocator overhead. Helpful symbols: × means multiplication, ÷ means division, [rows, columns] states a tensor shape, and a token row is one position in a text sequence. Each byte count and score is specific to the example, not a measured production model. Practise the calculation Question: Calculate raw K+V bytes for L=2, T=6 and C=8. Show the worked answer 2 × 2 × 6 × 8 × 4 = 768 bytes. Connect the idea to native C23 Use UmiAiTrainingStackedKvStoreInspect to compare the calculated raw tensor budget with Framework-reported reserved K/V bytes; not total process RAM. The actual mathematical implementation remains in Umicom Framework. The connected native Transformer learning path applies this principle to a bounded real-model experiment. A query is a vector which scores retained keys. Within one attention head, raw score is the dot product of query and key divided by sqrt(head width). Softmax turns scores into nonnegative weights summing to one. A fully worked example Use head width 2; query q=[1,0], keys k0=[1,0] and k1=[0,1]. Scaled scores are 1/sqrt(2) ≈0.7071 and 0. Let the associated values be v0=[2,0], v1=[0,4]. Their softmax weights are approximately [0.6698,0.3302]; output is [1.3396,1.3208]. Each byte count and score is specific to the example, not a measured production model. Practise the calculation Question: If both scaled scores are equal, what weight does each of the two keys receive? Show the worked answer Softmax gives 0.5 to each key, regardless of the common score. Exponentials become very large for large positive logits. A stable softmax subtracts the maximum score before taking exponentials; subtracting the same constant from all scores does not change their normalised ratios. A fully worked example For scores [1000,1001], direct exp may overflow ordinary FP32. Subtract 1001 to obtain [-1,0]. Exponentials are approximately [0.3679,1]. Dividing by 1.3679 yields probabilities [0.2689,0.7311]. Helpful symbols: × means multiplication, ÷ means division, [rows, columns] states a tensor shape, and a token row is one position in a text sequence. Each byte count and score is specific to the example, not a measured production model. Practise the calculation Question: Stabilise logits [5,7,7] by subtracting their maximum. Show the worked answer Subtract 7: [-2,0,0]. Their exponentials are [0.1353,1,1], which sum to 2.1353. Layer normalisation subtracts the mean of a token’s feature values and divides by sqrt(variance+epsilon), then applies learned scale and bias. It acts independently on each token row. A fully worked example For values [1,3], mean=2. Deviations are [-1,+1], population variance=(1+1)/2=1. With epsilon 0, normalised values are [-1,+1]; with small positive epsilon they become slightly closer to zero. With scale gamma=[1,1] and bias beta=[0,0], nothing further changes. Helpful symbols: × means multiplication, ÷ means division, [rows, columns] states a tensor shape, and a token row is one position in a text sequence. Each byte count and score is specific to the example, not a measured production model. Practise the calculation Question: Calculate the mean of [2,4,6,8] and name the deviations. Show the worked answer Mean=5, deviations=[-3,-1,+1,+3]. Their mean squared deviation is (9+1+1+9)/4=5. Connect the idea to native C23 Use precisely the canonical LayerNorm epsilon and FP32 conversion; changing epsilon changes every downstream Q/K/V projection. Could moving a bias through ReLU preserve every output? Show the worked answer ReLU returns [0,0,2.5]. Moving a bias generally changes which values are positive and therefore is not algebraically equivalent. What will you learn? Calculate a running softmax numerator without materialising every normalised score. ← Unit 19 · Maths homeA journey through two calculationsSuppose a banking risk score is calculated by doubling an input and then squaring the result. A mathematical model can have the same structure: the output from one operation becomes the input of another.u = 2w; L = u²w is the original number (a weight); u is an intermediate result; L is the final loss; the superscript ² means multiply a number by itself.At w=3, u=2×3=6 and L=6×6=36.Chain rule without mysterydL/dw = (dL/du) × (du/dw)The expression dL/du asks how fast loss changes with u; it equals 2u. The expression du/dw asks how fast u changes with w; it equals 2. Multiply: at u=6, gradient dL/dw = 12×2 = 24. Small changes in w therefore cause about 24 times that change in L near w=3.Why does this matter for a tensor?A tensor holds numbers in a structured array. A tensor operation transforms one or more arrays. During backpropagation, the Framework follows the graph of those operations in reverse order and accumulates all the different routes by which a weight influences the loss.PracticeRepeat with w=2. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation Author: Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Explain why a classifier produces logits rather than probabilities, calculate stable softmax probabilities, calculate the loss for one next-token target, and understand why low-rank adapter training can minimise exactly the same objective. 1. From scores to probabilities Suppose a toy language model predicts one of three symbols: A, B or C. Its raw logits are [2, 1, 0]. A logit is a numerical score that does not need to be nonnegative or add to one. Softmax converts logits into a probability distribution: P(i) = exp(zᵢ − m) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ − m) Here zᵢ is the logit for choice i; m is the largest logit; exp is the exponential function; Σ means sum across all choices. Subtracting the maximum improves numerical stability without changing the probabilities. For [2, 1, 0], subtract m = 2 to obtain [0, −1, −2]. Their exponentials are approximately [1, 0.367879, 0.135335]; the total is 1.503214. Divide each by that total: Token Approximate probability A 0.66524 B 0.24473 C 0.09003 The values add to one up to rounding. The largest score corresponds to the most probable token, but this does not prove it is factually correct. 2. How cross-entropy measures one prediction Assume B was the actual next token. The negative log-likelihood is: L = −ln(P(B)) ≈ −ln(0.24473) ≈ 1.408. L is loss. ln is the natural logarithm. A model that assigns more probability to the observed target receives a lower loss. If we had observed A instead, the loss would be approximately −ln(0.66524) = 0.408. For N training positions, mean cross-entropy is: L_mean = (1 / N) × Σₜ −ln(P(targetₜ)). Each position needs an explicit target token ID. If an application needs assistant-response-only loss, it must supply a separately qualified masking policy; simply averaging every position also trains on prompt-token predictions. 3. Why the Framework's tape matters In C23, the Umicom training tape owns logits, the stable cross-entropy calculation and reverse-mode differentiation. Applications do not reimplement softmax gradients. The canonical operation is: UmiAiTrainingTensor *loss = NULL; UmiStatus status = UmiAiTrainingCrossEntropy( tape, logitsTensor, targetIds, tokenCount, &loss); This is an excerpt; tape, logitsTensor and targetIds are already-created, caller-owned handles or arrays. After a successful forward and loss computation, UmiAiTrainingBackward(tape, loss) calculates gradients. The optimiser then updates only the parameters explicitly designated trainable. 4. Practice and worked answer Suppose a two-choice model produces equal logits [0, 0]. Each probability is 0.5. What is the loss when the target is the first choice? Answer: L = −ln(0.5) ≈ 0.693147. If the target probability increases to 0.8, its loss decreases to −ln(0.8) ≈ 0.223144. Cross-entropy rewards a better assigned probability, not merely an unchanged top-1 prediction. Important distinction: lower training loss does not demonstrate improved generalisation. An evaluation split built from genuinely held-out source documents must be measured separately. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation Author: Sammy Hegab Learning objectives Understand a rank-limited matrix product, compute a low-rank residual step by step and explain why a trainable output adapter can change predictions while its original decoder weights remain frozen. 1. An ordinary matrix can be expensive to change A dense matrix mapping 100 inputs to 100 outputs contains 100 × 100 = 10,000 weights. Training all those weights requires gradients and often optimiser state for every element. Instead of updating the original matrix, we can learn two smaller matrices: D has shape [inputChannels, rank]. U has shape [rank, outputChannels]. The product D × U has the original [inputChannels, outputChannels] shape. For rank 4, the two trainable matrices need 100×4 + 4×100 = 800 weights: 92% fewer than 10,000. This counts trainable weights only. It does not include temporary activations, gradients, checkpoint metadata or the still-retained frozen base model. 2. Worked example with two numbers Let the input be row vector x = [2, 1]. Choose a rank-one down matrix: D = [ 0.5 ] [−0.2 ] The reduced value is xD = 2×0.5 + 1×(−0.2) = 0.8. Let the up matrix be U = [0.1, −0.3]. The low-rank residual is: (xD)U = 0.8×[0.1, −0.3] = [0.08, −0.24]. Suppose the frozen base output is [1.5, 0.5]. Add the residual: adaptedOutput = [1.5, 0.5] + [0.08, −0.24] = [1.58, 0.26]. The base has not changed. Only the adapter controls how much is added. 3. What this means for a language-model head A language model normally emits logits for each token position. In the new bounded teaching experiment, the existing Umicom decoder produces a matrix of frozen logits Z of shape [tokenCount, vocabularySize]. A separate adapter applies: Z_adapted = Z + (Z × D) × U. For vocabulary size 260, adapter rank 4, the trainable count is 260×4 + 4×260 = 2,080. A dense 260×260 transformation would need 67,600 trainable weights. The residual adapter uses approximately 96.9% fewer weights for this output transformation. This is not the same operation as inserting LoRA into each Transformer attention projection. It is an experimental logit-residual head. The decoder remains an unchanged feature producer; the adapter learns only a correction to its output scores. Calling the two methods identical would confuse distinct model architectures. 4. Why the up matrix often begins at zero At creation, the Framework can initialise U = 0. Then (Z × D) × U = 0, so the adapted output initially equals the original decoder output. After backpropagation and optimiser updates, the residual may become nonzero. This gives a useful test: before any training, compare the output of the original decoder with the adapter's output. 5. Exercise with answer A frozen projection maps 32 input channels to 64 outputs, using rank 8. Calculate dense versus low-rank trainable weights. Answer: a dense matrix has 32×64 = 2,048 elements. Down matrix 32×8 = 256; up matrix 8×64 = 512; combined 768, a reduction of 2,048 − 768 = 1,280 or 62.5%. The reduction is smaller than in a 100×100 example because the selected rank is proportionally larger. Takeaway: parameter efficiency is a property of the matrix shapes. Model quality still requires measured held-out evaluation and correct lifetime rules. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation Author: Sammy Hegab Purpose Learn to calculate the shapes and parameter counts of a low-rank adapter before writing C23. This unit accompanies native Transformer projection adaptation. No advanced mathematics is required: only multiplication, addition and a basic understanding of matrices. 1. What does a dense projection do? A row of I input values is multiplied by a matrix containing I rows and O columns. The result contains O output values. The full weight matrix has: denseParameters = I × O For four inputs and six outputs, the dense matrix contains 4 × 6 = 24 values. Their units are parameters, not bytes. If each value occupies four bytes, the weight data occupy 24 × 4 = 96 bytes, excluding graph and storage metadata. 2. Use two narrow matrices instead A low-rank adapter adds a trainable correction without replacing the dense weights. Choose a small rank r: A: [I, r] B: [r, O] X: [N, I] XA: [N, r] (XA)B: [N, O] The adapter has I×r + r×O = r×(I+O) trainable numbers. With I=4, O=6, r=2, this is 8+12=20. The original 24 dense values are retained but need not be updated during adapter training. Notice that the example saves only four trainable values compared with training the entire dense matrix. For narrow toy networks, low rank may provide little benefit; its practical advantage grows with wider projections. 3. A more realistic numerical comparison Suppose a projection has 128 inputs, 256 outputs and rank 8: Full dense matrix: 128 × 256 = 32,768 weights Adapter down matrix: 128 × 8 = 1,024 weights Adapter up matrix: 8 × 256 = 2,048 weights Total adapter trainables: = 3,072 weights The adapter has 3,072 / 32,768 = 0.09375, or 9.375% as many trainable parameters as that one dense projection. This does not mean the total model occupies 9.375% of its previous memory: the frozen dense weights still exist. Optimiser moments, gradients and temporary activations add further memory costs. 4. Why a zero-initialised matrix matters Write the adapted result as Y = XW + (XA)B. At creation, B is zero. The correction (XA)B is then zero and the initial output is XW. This is a useful regression invariant: an untrained adapter must not unexpectedly alter the established model. Once training changes B, the correction can become nonzero. Gradients may subsequently update both narrow matrices. All of those calculations remain inside the Framework training tape; educational applications should use the public API rather than implement an independent neural engine. Practice Calculate the dense parameter count when I=64, O=64. Calculate adapter parameters when I=64, O=64, r=4. Explain why a small adapter count does not mean the frozen dense weights can be discarded. What is the output shape of an [8,128] input multiplied by a [128,8] adapter-down matrix and then an [8,256] adapter-up matrix? Worked answers 64×64 = 4,096. 64×4 + 4×64 = 512, which is 12.5% of the dense weight count. The correction adds to the original dense result; inference still needs the original weights. The intermediate shape is [8,8]; the final correction shape is [8,256]. Further study: Matrices and shapes, Gradient descent and Unit 24 — Gradients through a low-rank residual. ← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation Author: Sammy Hegab Purpose Understand how changing two small matrices can improve an adapted projection while the original dense matrix stays frozen. The Transformer adaptation lesson uses this principle in the existing C23 training tape. 1. Start with a scalar teaching model Before matrices, use simple numbers. Suppose the output is: y = xw + (xa)b Here x=2 is the input, w=3 is the frozen base weight, and a and b are the two trainable adapter values. If a=0.5 and b=0, then: base output = 2 × 3 = 6 adapter correction = (2 × 0.5) × 0 = 0 y = 6 The initial adapter leaves the original prediction unchanged. 2. Follow the gradient backwards Let the target be t=7 and loss be L=(y−t)²/2. Initially y=6, so L=(−1)²/2 = 0.5 and ∂L/∂y = y−t = −1. Apply the chain rule to the adapter weights: ∂y/∂a = xb ∂y/∂b = xa ∂L/∂a = (y−t) × xb ∂L/∂b = (y−t) × xa With x=2, a=0.5, b=0, the gradients are: ∂L/∂a = −1 × 2 × 0 = 0 ∂L/∂b = −1 × 2 × 0.5 = −1 The first update changes b, not a, because the correction's output is initially multiplied by zero. This does not mean a is permanently unable to train; after b changes, its gradient can become nonzero. 3. Make one SGD update Choose learning rate α=0.1 and subtract α×gradient from each trainable parameter: new a = 0.5 − 0.1×0 = 0.5 new b = 0 − 0.1×(−1) = 0.1 Now recompute the complete output: y = (2 × 3) + (2 × 0.5 × 0.1) = 6.1 L = (6.1 − 7)²/2 = 0.405 Loss fell from 0.5 to 0.405 in this one example. That is evidence for a particular training update, not proof that an adapted language model generalises to unseen source code. 4. Extend the idea to matrices For matrices the same expression is: Y = XW + (XA)B The chain rule uses matrix multiplication and transposes. If G is the derivative of loss with respect to Y, then the adapter gradients use: ∂L/∂A = Xᵀ G Bᵀ ∂L/∂B = (XA)ᵀ G The dimensions are important. With X:[N,I], A:[I,r], B:[r,O] and G:[N,O]: Xᵀ G Bᵀ : [I,N] × [N,O] × [O,r] = [I,r] (XA)ᵀ G : [r,N] × [N,O] = [r,O] Those are precisely the shapes of A and B. The real Framework uses automatic differentiation to calculate the gradients; the equations give learners an independent way to reason about them. 5. Why freezing the base matters The original weight W contributes to the forward computation but does not belong in the adapter-only optimiser parameter list. Its values must be unchanged before and after each training step. The Framework's low-rank trainable selector returns A and B only, and the tape's multi-parameter SGD writer checks a complete candidate update before committing either matrix. A numerical regression should check both sides: the new adapter learns and the frozen base does not change. Practice Recalculate the scalar example if the target is 5 rather than 7. What is the initial sign of ∂L/∂b? Why does ∂L/∂a start at zero when b=0? Check the shape of ∂L/∂B for N=8, I=128, r=8, O=256. Explain why two sets of trainable adapter weights must be updated consistently, rather than publishing only the first successful write. Worked answers y−t = +1, so ∂L/∂b = +1. The product xb is zero, so the immediate correction is insensitive to a. [8,256], the same shape as the adapter-up matrix. A partially updated pair would represent neither the previous model nor the intended complete optimiser step. Further study: Unit 20 — Matrix chain rule and Unit 23 — Parameter counts. Learning outcome Calculate, check and interpret one quantity used in a native distributed-learning system. Separate mathematical assumptions, theoretical bounds, reserved metadata and actual measured performance. Step-by-step worked calculation A job has 96 KiB admission budget. Worker A requests 50 KiB and B 50 KiB. 50+50=100 KiB >96 KiB, so B cannot be admitted concurrently. After A completes, its reserved 50 KiB is released and B may enter. If only one is pending at a time, peak reserved bytes =50×1,024=51,200 bytes; cumulative declared requests across both workers =102,400 bytes. Application to a C23 learning network A robust implementation checks dimensions and integer bounds before modifying stored state. The existing Framework federated aggregation and new job-admission services treat sample counts, model vectors and transfer reservations as different units. None of the arithmetic presented here proves that remote training was carried out honestly. Independent exercise Question: If C requests 40 KiB while B is pending at 50 KiB, will C fit? Give the reserved total in KiB. Reveal the complete solution Yes: 50+40=90 KiB ≤96 KiB. The difference 6 KiB remains available. These are declared forecasts, not measured traffic. Units, assumptions and interpretation Preserve byte versus bit, decimal MB versus binary MiB, sample count versus token count, and reported resource forecasts versus observed measurements. If the calculation describes a statistical model, state its independence assumptions; if it describes a rejected update, do not silently change the aggregation algorithm. Further study Related LLM Lesson 393 · Mathematics learning path. Service to Many Leads to Greatness.

← PreviousNext →Continuation catalogueCourse home Umicom Foundation · Author: Sammy Hegab Prerequisites: Variables and functions, cross-entropy 1. A model predicts what comes next An autoregressive decoder receives token tᵢ and predicts the following token tᵢ₊₁. The subscript i means a position in a sequence. During teacher-forced training the real preceding tokens are supplied, rather than using the model's earlier guesses. Suppose a prompt is AB and a response is C. Write the full sequence with special tokens: [BOS, A, B, C, EOS] We train on next-token pairs, not token copies. At position 0, the input is BOS and the target is A; at position 1, A → B; at position 2, B → C; at position 3, C → EOS. 2. A mask selects the answer If A and B are prompt context, the model does not need to receive loss for predicting them in this response-only exercise. The two desired targets are C and EOS. We therefore assign mask values [0,0,1,1] for the four next-token pairs. A mask value 1 means include this row's loss; 0 means exclude it. Let mᵢ be a mask, pᵢ the predicted probability of the correct target at position i, and Lᵢ = −ln(pᵢ) the corresponding negative log-likelihood. The selected mean is: L(selected) = (Σᵢ mᵢ Lᵢ) / (Σᵢ mᵢ). The denominator counts selected targets. It is not the total number of sequence positions. All-zero masks must be refused because division by zero has no defined training meaning. 3. Worked probability example Suppose the model assigns 0.80 probability to C and 0.50 probability to EOS in the two selected positions: −ln(0.80) ≈ 0.2231. −ln(0.50) ≈ 0.6931. Mean selected loss: (0.2231 + 0.6931) / 2 ≈ 0.4581. Changing either prompt-only loss does not change this particular selected mean, because the corresponding mask is zero. The prompt still influences the hidden states and predictions at the selected rows: ignored loss does not mean ignored input context. 4. What changes when the context is padded? If the decoder expects eight inputs but the meaningful stream contains fewer tokens, right-padding positions receive PAD tokens. Their target mask remains zero. A loss on padding might teach the model to predict padding rather than useful answers. The full reviewed prompt and completion must fit within the context. Truncating an answer but leaving an apparently valid EOS loss would create misleading training evidence. 5. Practice and answers Practice: A sequence contains five next-token targets, with mask [0,1,0,1,1]. How many losses enter the average? Answer: 3. Practice: Selected probabilities are 1/2, 1/4, and 1/2. Calculate the average negative log-likelihood. Answer: −(ln(1/2) + ln(1/4) + ln(1/2))/3 ≈ (0.6931 + 1.3863 + 0.6931)/3 ≈ 0.9242. Practice: Why is the first response target paired with the final prompt input token? Answer: the model always predicts the token after the current input position. Connect to the C23 Framework Study the byte-window laboratory, then selected-token cross-entropy. Both use the established Umicom Framework tokenizer, tape and loss semantics.
